notes: 14 acts on 2 stages over 2 days for a 65-pound-a-day roots festival keepsake booklet: a 2-page 2025 programme PDF whose profile page has the portrait FLATTENED into the page (zero graphic frames, name+stage+time+bio as one continuous flow) so it looks best but cannot carry a per-act photo; the plainer 2023 profile PDF that CAN (genuinely placed image, separated frames) but whose portrait frame is close to SQUARE and much smaller than the print implies while the press photos are wide landscape stage frames, plus a fixed-height bio frame that oversets long bios mid-sentence at trim while the merge reports complete, and a lossy readout so the mapping must be reconstructed from the document's own content runs; 14 press photos from 14 hands (1 neutral daylight reference, 2 magenta stage washes that go green on a global neutral push, 2 narrow-lit-band black-stage frames where a subject crop locks onto a chrome mic stand / monitor wedge and clips the face, 1 oversharpened saturated phone-preset frame that fights correction, 1 low-res over-compressed website save, plus cool/warm and off-level phone grabs; commissioned frames delivered at 6000x4000 to trip oversize/silent-downscale and the no-upscale bar); a phone photo of the painted gate banner carrying the compound crest (hanging lantern with glazing bars inside a laurel ring under an arched wordmark, two paints on weathered cream canvas, paint bled into the weave so counters close at page size, an enclosed laurel ring background-removal returns as an opaque disc, and the wordmark reads dominant so a whole-crest prompt silently drops the lantern and ring); a 14-row lineup CSV in BOOKING order (neither day nor set-time order, which is exactly what sets page order) with wildly uneven bios (one two-sentence, three near-double last year's longest) bound to the 14 photos through an @-prefixed image column; and a clean committee note giving the two stage names, the two headliners that must close their day, the licence line that must appear verbatim, and the 23 September printer deadline.

Faded weathered outdoor canvas, visible coarse weave, chips and fading, a casual real-world reference snapshot, not a studio shot. LAYOUT SPEC for last year's printed programme, TWO pages held by the printer (the cover plus one performer profile page), to be converted to a live document downstream. Real embedded font subsets.

Document: A5 portrait booklet, 148 x 210 mm per page, TWO pages, fonts embedded as real subsets, NO bleed box present (trim = media box, 0 mm bleed). This is the newer, handsomer design the committee likes best and asked to use.

PAGE 1 - COVER (what it looks like printed):
- Full-bleed weathered-cream ground (#EFE6D2).
- The painted crest large and centred near the top: a hanging lantern inside a laurel ring under an arched wordmark, reproduced from the gate banner.
- Festival name LANTERNWOOD FOLK FEST in a warm serif display face, large.
- Tagline 'Two days of roots on the farm' beneath.
- Year and weekend dates at the foot in a clean sans.

PAGE 2 - PERFORMER PROFILE PAGE (what it looks like printed):
- A large portrait photograph of the act filling roughly the upper two thirds of the page.
- The ACT NAME in a warm serif, large, below the photograph.
- A STAGE / DAY / SET TIME line in a clean sans, small, under the name.
- A BIOGRAPHY in a body serif beneath that.
- The crest small in a bottom corner.

HOW PAGE 2 IS ACTUALLY SET (the reverse-engineering trap):
- The portrait was NOT placed as an image. The previous designer FLATTENED it into the page, so it lives in the page content as a baked-in raster rather than a placed graphic. On conversion the page therefore exposes ZERO graphic frames, and there is nothing for a per-act photograph to bind into, however plainly the printed page shows a photograph.
- The ACT NAME, the STAGE/DAY/SET TIME line and the BIOGRAPHY are ONE continuous text story in a SINGLE text frame, not three addressable frames, so stage, set time and biography cannot be mapped to separate fields.
- The conversion reports no problem at all: it round-trips cleanly and looks identical to the usable 2023 page. The unusable-ness is invisible from the printed page and appears in no error; it is only visible once the frame inventory is read out of the round-tripped IDML.

FIELD LABELS the downstream mapping would need (present as content, not as addressable tokens): ACT_NAME | STAGE | DAY | SET_TIME | BIOGRAPHY | PORTRAIT | CREST

Colours: Weathered Cream #EFE6D2 ground, Barn Charcoal #2C2823 body text, Lantern Amber #C6822E act name, Field Green #3B5137 stage/time line.

assets.defect_engineered: the plainer page the committee likes LESS but that CAN carry the job: the portrait is a genuinely PLACED image in a real graphic frame and the name/stage-time/biography are SEPARATE frames; BUT the portrait frame is close to SQUARE (~52x56 mm) and much smaller than the print implies while the press photos are wide landscape stage frames, so all fourteen must be cropped to a small near-square proportion set by this frame not by the print; and the BIOGRAPHY frame is a fixed-height, non-reflowing frame set tight to that year's short bios, so a longer biography oversets and ends MID-SENTENCE at trim while the merge reports every record complete; plus the readout drops a run so offsets must be reconstructed from the document's own content runs
assets.content:
LAYOUT SPEC for the programme from two years ago, ONE performer profile page, a plainer design by the same designer before he changed his layout. To be converted to a live document downstream. Real embedded font subsets.

Document: A5 portrait booklet page, 148 x 210 mm, single page, fonts embedded as real subsets, NO bleed box present (trim = media box, 0 mm bleed). The committee included this one only 'in case it helps' and thinks it less handsome.

WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE PRINTED (appears to be four tidy blocks):
- A portrait photograph of the act, which on the printed page reads as large and near-portrait.
- The ACT NAME in a warm serif, large.
- A STAGE / DAY / SET TIME line in a clean sans.
- A BIOGRAPHY in a body serif.
- The crest small at the foot.

HOW IT IS ACTUALLY SET (this is the page that CAN carry the job, with two catches):
- The portrait IS a genuinely PLACED image sitting in a real graphic frame, so a per-act photograph can bind here. BUT that graphic frame is close to SQUARE and considerably SMALLER than the printed page suggests: roughly 52 x 56 mm, seated in the upper third, not the tall near-full-page photograph the print implies. The press photographs are wide LANDSCAPE stage frames, so every one of the fourteen must be cropped to this small near-square proportion, driven by the frame's real bounds and not by what either printed page appears to show.
- The ACT NAME, the STAGE/DAY/SET TIME line and the BIOGRAPHY are SEPARATE, individually addressable text frames. This is exactly why this page works where the newer one does not.
- BUT the BIOGRAPHY frame is a FIXED-HEIGHT frame set tight to that year's short biographies, with no auto-size and no overflow or reflow. A biography longer than that year's stops rendering partway and ends MID-SENTENCE at trim, while the merge reports every record complete. Three of this year's biographies run to nearly double the longest of that year, so they overset silently.
- Note on the story text: the mapping readout reconstructs the frame's text conveniently, but a dropped content run leaves every later character offset short; offsets must be computed from the document's OWN content runs, not from the readout, or the placeholders land in the wrong place while the validator returns valid.

FIELD LABELS the downstream mapping must resolve (present as content, not as visible tokens): ACT_NAME | STAGE | DAY | SET_TIME | BIOGRAPHY | PORTRAIT | CREST

Colours: Weathered Cream #EFE6D2 ground, Barn Charcoal #2C2823 body text, Laurel Deep #1F3A2E act name, Lantern Amber #C6822E rule lines.

assets.defect_engineered: 14 rows in BOOKING order (neither day order nor set-time order), which is exactly what determines page order in the finished booklet, so keeping the sheet order buries both headliners (rows 3 and 9) mid-list; biographies are wildly uneven because each act wrote its own (Delia Marsh is two sentences; The Hollow Pines, Marla Vance & the Tallgrass and The Bramble Sisters each run to nearly double the longest of last year, so they overset the 2023 page's tight biography frame); the @Image column binds each act to its own press photo by exact filename

Act Name,Stage,Day,Set Time,Biography,@Image
Cole Harrow Band,The Barn Stage,Saturday,6:00pm,"A four-piece out of Bristol trading in swampy, foot-stomping Americana. Slide guitar, a Hammond organ that has seen things, and a rhythm section that does not stop. They played the late slot last year and we asked them straight back.",lanternwood_press_photo_03.jpg
Rue & the Ravens,The Orchard Stage,Sunday,1:00pm,"Dark, gothic folk from the edge of the moor. A cello, a harmonium, close harmonies and songs about the sea taking people. Beautiful and a little haunting, and exactly right for a Sunday afternoon.",lanternwood_press_photo_12.jpg
The Hollow Pines,The Barn Stage,Saturday,9:00pm,"The Hollow Pines have spent the better part of a decade turning small rooms into something close to church. What began as two brothers harmonising over a single guitar at a kitchen table in the Mendips has grown, slowly and stubbornly, into a five-piece that can fill a field without ever raising its voice too far. Their songs are built from the ordinary business of staying somewhere: the drive home in the dark, the field you grew up beside, the people who leave and the people who do not. Three albums in, they have earned a following that treats every show like a reunion, singing the choruses back word for word before the band has finished them. We have wanted them at Lanternwood since the very first year, and we are proud beyond all measure to have them close the Saturday night. Bring a voice. You are going to be using it.",lanternwood_press_photo_04.jpg
Delia Marsh,The Barn Stage,Sunday,2:00pm,"Delia plays the harp and sings like the room has gone quiet even when it has not. Her debut record came out this spring.",lanternwood_press_photo_08.jpg
Fenwick & Doon,The Orchard Stage,Saturday,1:00pm,"A duo, a fiddle and a battered parlour guitar, and two voices that have been finishing each other's lines for twenty years. Traditional tunes, mostly, played the way they were meant to be. You will be dancing whether you meant to or not.",lanternwood_press_photo_05.jpg
The Copper Kettles,The Barn Stage,Sunday,4:00pm,"A skiffle revival band who take it all extremely seriously and not seriously at all, in equal measure. Washboard, tea-chest bass, and a kazoo when the mood takes them. Deeply silly, genuinely brilliant, and a great deal of fun.",lanternwood_press_photo_09.jpg
Odessa Frame,The Barn Stage,Saturday,4:00pm,"Odessa writes quiet songs and sings them louder than you expect. She has toured the folk clubs for six years with just a guitar and a suitcase, and this is her first festival main stage. Come early; she opens gently.",lanternwood_press_photo_02.jpg
Ambrose Fell,The Orchard Stage,Sunday,5:00pm,"Ambrose is a one-man band in the proper sense: kick drum, guitar, harmonica and a stomp box, running the whole thing himself. Ragged, joyful, and much bigger than it has any right to be. A brilliant way to close the Orchard Stage.",lanternwood_press_photo_14.jpg
Marla Vance & the Tallgrass,The Barn Stage,Sunday,8:30pm,"There are voices you hear and voices you feel in your chest, and Marla Vance has spent thirty years proving she has the second kind. She came up singing in touring roadhouse bands long before anyone was writing her name at the top of a poster, and she has never once forgotten what a live room is actually for. The Tallgrass, her band of many years, read her like weather, swelling and dropping back so that the songs breathe around her. Together they make music that manages to sound brand new and like something you have always somehow known, all dust and warmth with a low ache running underneath it. To have her closing our Sunday, out in a field, as the last of the light goes, is the exact thing this committee dreamed about when we started the festival on nothing but nerve and a borrowed marquee. Do not miss a second of it. Stay for the very last note.",lanternwood_press_photo_11.jpg
The Salt Marsh Ramblers,The Barn Stage,Saturday,2:00pm,"Five friends from the Levels who have been playing pub back rooms and barn dances since school. Fiddle, banjo, guitar, double bass and a great deal of shouting. Expect reels, murder ballads and at least one song about flooding.",lanternwood_press_photo_01.jpg
Junction Road Revival,The Orchard Stage,Saturday,5:00pm,"Six of them, three horns, and absolutely no interest in you standing still. Junction Road Revival play gospel soul and old rhythm and blues like the roof is already coming off. If your feet hurt on Sunday morning, this is why.",lanternwood_press_photo_07.jpg
The Threshing Floor,The Orchard Stage,Sunday,3:00pm,"A young band making very old music sound urgent again. Bouzouki, fiddle, bodhran and a frontman whose stories between songs are almost as good as the songs. Ones to watch, and you saw them here.",lanternwood_press_photo_13.jpg
The Bramble Sisters,The Orchard Stage,Saturday,3:00pm,"The Bramble Sisters are not sisters, and only one of them is called Bramble, but the name stuck the way the good ones do. The three of them met singing in a chapel choir and discovered, somewhere between the hymns, that their voices did something strange and lovely when they leaned into a minor chord together. For eight years now they have carried that sound around the country, unaccompanied for whole songs at a time, letting three voices do the work of a full band. Their set moves from old shape-note hymns to their own writing and back again without ever quite telling you where the seam was. It is the kind of thing that can stop a noisy field halfway through a sentence. We have put them on the Orchard Stage in the afternoon light entirely on purpose. Find a bale of hay, sit yourself down, and let them get to work on you.",lanternwood_press_photo_06.jpg
Waylon Pike Trio,The Barn Stage,Sunday,6:00pm,"Waylon Pike has been playing guitar longer than most of the committee has been alive, and it shows in every unhurried note. With brush drums and an upright bass behind him, the trio plays a warm, late-afternoon kind of blues. Perfect for the graveyard slot between lunch and the headliner.",lanternwood_press_photo_10.jpg

LANTERNWOOD FOLK FEST - committee note to the designer (everything else you need from us)

TICKETS
Sixty-five pounds a day. Two thousand capacity, two stages, fourteen acts across the weekend. Weekend and day tickets both. Under sixteens free with a paying adult.

THE TWO STAGES (please use these exact names on every page and both boards)
- The Barn Stage (the big one, in the old threshing barn)
- The Orchard Stage (the smaller one, out in the orchard by the cider tent)

THE HEADLINERS (this one matters)
Saturday is closed by The Hollow Pines on The Barn Stage.
Sunday is closed by Marla Vance & the Tallgrass on The Barn Stage.
Those two are the reason a lot of people bought a ticket. Whatever running order you settle on, they have to READ as the headliners, closing their own day, not buried in the middle of a list because that is where our spreadsheet happened to put them. Please do not sequence them as though they are just two more acts.

RUNNING ORDER
The line-up sheet is in the order we booked people, which is NOT the order the weekend runs in. The programme has to run in the order the acts actually go on, so someone standing in the field can find who is on next. Two stages running at the same time makes that a judgement rather than a plain sort, so tell us in the note how you decided.

THE LICENCE LINE (must appear in the programme, word for word)
'Lanternwood Folk Fest is run under a Temporary Event Notice granted by Mendip District Council (ref TEN/26/0912). Please drink responsibly and look after the field - it is a working farm and we would like to be asked back.'

THE DEADLINE
The printer needs the press file by Wednesday 23 September. They want three working days after that, so the 23rd is hard, not hopeful. If something cannot be done in time, tell us now, not on the 22nd.

AND
Please tell us anything you find that we should know before it goes to print. We would far rather hear it from you than find it framed on a kitchen wall.
